analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil, chemicals, and corporate income to fund toxic-waste cleanup.
analysis.headline: A bill to make polluting industries pay again for Superfund toxic-site cleanup was introduced in 2017 with 3 Democratic sponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. From 1980 to 1995, that cleanup was funded by taxes on oil, petrochemicals, and large corporate income — the "polluter pays" principle. Those taxes lapsed in 1995, leaving cleanup to be paid from general taxpayer money. This bill would have brought the taxes back through the end of 2021: an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products, a tax on chemical feedstocks, and a corporate environmental income tax of 0.12% on large corporations' alternative minimum taxable income above $2 million.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near the country's roughly 1,300 toxic waste sites, communities where cleanup has slowed for lack of money, and taxpayers generally, who since 1995 have borne cleanup costs that polluting industries once paid into the Superfund trust fund.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on crude oil, petroleum products, and chemicals, directing that revenue into the Superfund trust fund that pays for cleaning up the nation's most contaminated sites.

It also reinstates the corporate environmental income tax — 0.12% on a large corporation's alternative minimum taxable income above $2 million — through 2021, restoring an industry-financed revenue stream for the program.
The bill removes the exemption for petroleum exported from the United States, so refiners shipping crude and products abroad also contribute to the fund.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and petrochemical manufacturers, which pay the excise taxes, and large corporations generally, which pay the environmental income tax — with some of those costs likely passed to consumers in fuel and chemical prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners, chemical makers, large corporations

drawbacks.text: The corporate environmental income tax is not limited to polluting firms: it applies to any large corporation's income above $2 million, so companies that never contaminated a site would also pay into the fund.
Excise taxes on crude oil and petroleum products are largely passed through to consumers in the form of slightly higher fuel prices, an energy-price effect an honest supporter must acknowledge.
The $2 million exemption threshold is fixed rather than inflation-adjusted, which over time sweeps in ever more mid-sized firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is modestly higher fuel and chemical prices — much of which falls on the industries themselves — against a dedicated, industry-funded stream of money to clean toxic sites near homes and schools. The main design weakness is that the corporate income tax reaches corporations regardless of whether they polluted, diluting the pure "polluter pays" logic; but even with that caveat, the bill's costs are diffuse and small while its benefit is targeted cleanup of sites that threaten health.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died quietly when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on March 13, 2017, joined by Reps. Blumenauer and Pascrell, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — after the referral to committee.
The bill was never voted on in the House and was not taken up by the Senate before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies, and large corporations generally, avoided the reinstated taxes for the rest of the decade, while the cost of cleaning old toxic sites continued to fall on general taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies that avoided the taxes

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act to reinstate the Superfund financing taxes.

for.name: Reps. Earl Blumenauer and Bill Pascrell Jr.
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only two cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, but the bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were all Democrats, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never moved it.

industries.note: They would have paid the reinstated Superfund excise taxes on crude oil, petroleum products, and chemical feedstocks — including on exported petroleum. Since 1995 they have avoided this cost while taxpayers fund cleanup, so their interest in keeping the taxes expired runs against communities that live with toxic sites.

The corporate environmental income tax of 0.12% on alternative minimum taxable income above $2 million would apply to all large corporations, whether or not they polluted. It is a modest per-firm cost but funds cleanup that benefits the public.
Since the Superfund taxes lapsed, general taxpayer money has covered cleanup costs. Reinstating the polluter taxes would shift that burden back to industry and relieve the general fund.
